                                                PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                                       §          PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                                    §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561                                  §                          OF TEXAS

                  VISTRA CORPORATE SERVICES COMPANY’S COMMENTS

         Vistra Corporate Services Company (“Vistra”) respectfully submits these comments to
request a limited but important clarification to the Recommended Adoption Order in
Project No. 58481 (“RAO”), which was publicly released only two business days ago. The RAO
includes sweeping statements concerning the role of an interconnecting distribution service
provider (“DSP”) and a customer that are not consistent with settled Texas law and are thus worthy
of correction by the Commission. Those sweeping statements are offered as support for the RAO’s
rule language suggesting that a service relationship between a DSP and a large load customer is
universally required even if under current law no such service relationship is always necessary.
Vistra respectfully requests that the Commission consider these comments on the RAO and revise
the RAO to avoid any suggestion that a large load customer that is receiving lawful service under
current Texas law must itself be the DSP’s retail customer of record or must have any direct retail
delivery service relationship with the DSP.
         The RAO in Project No. 58481 broadly proposes to reject Vistra’s advocacy on the
proposed rule that the rule language should expressly recognize that not every large load customer
will take service from an interconnecting DSP. The RAO asserts that all large loads interconnected
to the ERCOT system must take retail electric delivery service from a DSP, and that it would be
“contrary to PURA1 and existing commission rules” and not “consistent with the overall
framework of PURA and existing commission rules in place since the deregulation of the ERCOT
market” for a load to not take retail electric delivery service from a DSP.2

         1
             Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”).
          2
            The RAO asserts that “all large load customers that interconnect to the ERCOT system must take service
from an interconnecting DSP.” (p. 66). It also states: “Consistent with the overall framework of PURA and existing
commission rules in place since the deregulation of the ERCOT market, a DSP is the appropriate entity with the
customer relationship and must necessarily be a party to the SLLIA. The commission declines to adopt a policy that
departs from this longstanding framework.” (pp. 68-69). There is a similar recitation on p. 70. And in rejecting Vistra’s
recommendation to require disclosure of whether retail electric delivery service from a DSP will occur, the RAO states
that “such a requirement suggests that a large load customer that co-locates with a generation resource does not have
to take retail electric delivery service from a DSP, which would be contrary to PURA and existing commission rules.”
(p. 105).

Vistra Comments on RAO
Project No. 58481                                                                                         Page 1 of 8
          Vistra recognizes that taking retail electric delivery service from a DSP is and has been the
predominant service model in the ERCOT market, but Texas statutes, Commission rules, and
Commission precedent expressly and implicitly recognize numerous arrangements in which
electricity is delivered to an interconnected customer, sometimes separately from and sometimes
through or even originating from the certificated utility’s system, but the entity that ultimately
consumes the electricity is not the utility’s customer of record and does not have a direct
distribution service relationship with that utility.3
         Furthermore, and critical to the scope of this rulemaking to implement PURA § 37.0561 as
enacted by 2025 Senate Bill No. 6 (“SB6”), neither PURA § 37.0561 specifically, nor SB6 more
generally, authorizes, directs, or motivates a departure from the settled law that has in many varied
instances allowed for lawful receipt of electricity by a consumer who has no service relationship
with a DSP. As a matter of fact, PURA § 39.169 expressly recognizes the co-location of large loads
with existing generators under current law. Current Texas law unambiguously allows receipt of
electricity by a consumer who has no service relationship with a DSP, in the situations described
herein and in other situations.
         The rule and the order adopting the rule should not create any confusion regarding the long-
standing lawfulness of such receipt of electricity. The Commission’s final order should not include
statements to the contrary and should recognize that a DSP is not always a necessary service
provider to large loads, for the reasons discussed herein. In addition to the established Texas law,
there are good policy reasons to recognize and preserve the continued ability to utilize those limited
exceptions—among those reasons are policy rationales that the Federal Energy Regulatory
Commission (“FERC”) has recently supported. Taking a different path in this rulemaking would
put Texas on track to be out of step with the rest of the country.

         3
           See e.g. Application of Central Power and Light Company for Declaratory Order, Docket No. 25395, Final
Order at 13 (June 21, 2004) (affirming customer may lawfully own wires to serve itself as the end user of electricity
delivered from a third-party generator) (“Flint Hills”); Complaint of Power Clearinghouse, Inc. Against the City of
Austin Electric Utility Department for Denial of Transmission Service, Docket No. 16147, Order Granting Motion to
Dismiss (Oct. 10, 1996) (“Power Clearinghouse”); Power Clearinghouse, Inc. v. Pub. Util. Comm'n of Tex., 968
S.W.2d 537 (Tex. App.—Austin 1998, no pet.) (affirming that a landlord may lawfully provide power to tenants
without the tenant having a direct relationship with the DSP); Petition of Big Country Electric Cooperative, Inc. for a
Cease and Desist Order, Docket No 35690, Final Order (Feb. 22, 2010) (approving of an arrangement where multiple
owners owned an on-site distribution system and only the unitized field operator, not the multiple owners, had a
relationship with the DSP) (“Big County”); Tex. Prop. Code §§92.301 and 92.302 (providing that in a master meter
arrangement there is a customer of the DSP that is separate from the end use consumers of electricity (i.e., the tenants));
PURA § 31.002(6)(J)(i); PURA § 31.002(6)(J)(ii); 16 TAC § 25.5(42)(J)(ii); 16 TAC § 25.109; PURA §
31.002(6)(J)(iii); 16 TAC § 25.501(m) (providing that wholesale storage load “is not subject to retail tariffs”).

Vistra Comments on RAO
Project No. 58481                                                                                           Page 2 of 8
          This issue is important particularly in the case of co-locating large loads with generation
resources. No involvement by a DSP is necessary to lawfully interconnect a large load behind a
generation resource’s point of interconnection (“POI”) or to implement a net metering arrangement
with that generation resource so long as the large load customer owns the transmission and
distribution (“T&D”) facilities that will deliver power from the generator’s substation to the large
load consuming facility. Such customer self-provision of T&D service is lawful non-utility T&D
service under PURA § 31.002(6)(J)(i) and Commission precedent, including the Flint Hills
decision. Further, even if the load receives grid power that is first delivered to the generation site
through the generator’s POI, if the generator is also the landowner/landlord to the large load tenant,
the generator/landlord may lawfully furnish that power to the large-load owner as an incident of
tenancy, consistent with PURA § 31.002(6)(J)(i) and Commission precedent, including the Power
Clearinghouse decision. There are no limitations in PURA to these lawful constructs. The large
load’s co-location at the generator’s site does not disallow the construct, nor does the mere size of
the load. The broad statements in the RAO contradict settled Texas law on this point: thus, it is
improper to inject this surprising and wholly unsupported statement of policy into this rulemaking,
especially at the tail end of a process in which this scope expansion was not proposed for public
comment as a material and general departure from existing law, and where parties were not
afforded the opportunity to fully brief the Commission regarding the current law and the potential
impacts of generalizations that depart from established Commission decisions and PURA.


    I.         PURA and Commission precedent make clear that not every end-use customer
               needs to have a relationship with a DSP.

         Texas law dictates that it is not necessary for a DSP to provide distribution service to a
large load for a proposed net metering arrangement to be lawful. In general, a person who owns or
operates facilities to transmit or distribute electricity is an electric utility,4 but Texas law provides
clear and applicable exceptions for customer-owned facilities and for provision of electricity by a
landlord to its tenant. While the general rule is that a retail electric utility may not furnish or make
available retail electric utility service in an area for which it does not hold a certificate,5 and,



         4
             PURA § 31.002(6).
         5
             PURA 37.051(b).

Vistra Comments on RAO
Project No. 58481                                                                           Page 3 of 8
 generally, the DSP is the electric utility who holds a certificate to provide retail delivery service
and the entity from whom an end-use customer obtains distribution service, there are exceptions
expressly stated in PURA and applied by Commission contested-case decisions.
         The Commission correctly applied PURA to allow a customer to own or operate
transmission or distribution facilities that indirectly interconnect to the ERCOT system by
connecting a third-party’s ERCOT-interconnected generator to the customer’s load without the
customer becoming an electric utility, in the Flint Hills decision.6 In fact, the Flint Hills decision
went a step further, concluding that it is lawful for multiple unrelated customers to jointly own
such T&D facilities as tenants-in-common.
         In this situation, a REP can purchase electricity at wholesale from a generator and sell it to
a customer that transmits the electricity from the generator to its load facilities over customer-
owned T&D facilities. A transaction of this type does not require a DSP, either physically or legally.
         The Commission also applied PURA’s “incident of tenancy” exception in the
Power Clearinghouse decision to confirm that a landlord may provide electric service to its tenant
as an incident of that tenancy.7 That is, a landlord’s facilities may interconnect to a DSP and the
landlord may even take retail delivery service from a DSP, but if the landlord’s contractual
relationship with its tenant includes the provision of (but not the resale of) electricity to the tenant,
then the tenant that ultimately consumes the electricity is not required to have a separate
interconnection or service relationship with a DSP. In a net metering arrangement between a
generator/landlord and large load customer/tenant, the large load customer can lawfully receive
power without any direct relationship with a DSP, and without any provision of retail delivery
service by a DSP to the large load customer.
         The Third Court of Appeals affirmed the Commission’s Order in Power Clearinghouse.8
The Court held that the sale of power to the landlord was not a wholesale transaction.9 Rather, the
landlord received power from the grid as a retail customer and provided it to its tenants. Thus, the



         6
             PURA § 31.002(6)(J)(i); Flint Hills, Final Order at 13 (Conclusion of Law No. 7).
         7
           PURA § 31.002(6)(J)(i); Complaint of Power Clearinghouse, Inc. Against the City of Austin Electric Utility
Department for Denial of Transmission Service, Docket No. 16147, Order Granting Motion to Dismiss (“Order”)
(Oct. 10, 1996) (“Power Clearinghouse”).
         8
             Power Clearinghouse, Inc. v. Pub. Util. Comm'n of Tex., 968 S.W.2d 537 (Tex. App.—Austin 1998, no pet.).
         9
             Power Clearinghouse, Inc., 968 S.W.2d 537 at 541.

Vistra Comments on RAO
Project No. 58481                                                                                      Page 4 of 8
 landlord was correctly considered to be receiving electricity as a retail customer and furnishing it,
not reselling it, to its tenant, as permitted by PURA.
        Power Clearinghouse is especially pertinent in the context of the RAO because it shows
that the distinction between the customer of the utility and the end-use consumer is not an
unintended loophole in current law. The Commission considered the actual physical connections
and contractual structure—utility facilities were connected to a master meter, a property owner
purchased utility service, the property owner owned private downstream distribution facilities, and
tenants consumed electricity delivered by the landlord over those facilities—and treated the utility
transaction with the property owner distinctly from the property owner/landlord’s relationship with
its tenants/consumers. 16 Tex. Admin. Code (“TAC”) § 25.142 provides a similar structure when
a landlord owns submeters. When the landlord owns submeters but the DSP owns the master meter,
electricity reaches and is consumed by the tenant, but the tenant is not the DSP’s customer, and the
tenant has no relationship with the DSP. Similarly, in 16 TAC § 25.141 and Tex. Prop.
Code § 92.302, the rule and statute expressly acknowledge that the person with the relationship
with the utility or REP is the “customer” of the utility, while the tenants are the end use consumers
of electricity.
        The provision of electricity as an incident of tenancy is not confined to residential
examples. Request of Trenton View Shopping Center, PUCT Docket No. 36349, and Application
of San Jacinto Mall Company Against Houston Power Lighting and Power Company, PUC Docket
No. 2822 both involve shopping malls providing power to their tenants as part of the landlord-
tenant relationship. In both of these proceedings, the Commission or Commission Staff determined
that there was no PURA violation associated with the provision of power to the tenants. The fact
patterns in these cases again make clear that the landlord had the direct relationship with the DSP
and the tenants were the ultimate consumers of the power.
        Further highlighting both the lawfulness of customer-owned distribution and the distinction
between the DSP customer and a different end-user, in a case known as “Big Country,” the
Commission found no concern with an electricity distribution system being jointly owned by
25 owners serving a unitized oil field operated by one operator who was the DSP’s customer.10
The Commission treated the operator of the unitized oil field as one customer (even though the


        10
             Big Country, Docket No 35690.

Vistra Comments on RAO
Project No. 58481                                                                       Page 5 of 8
 operator was only one of the 25 owners of the field), and ratified that operator’s operation of the
distribution system jointly owned by 25 different mineral working interest owners. 11 The
Commission did not require each well site, or each individual working interest owner, to take
distribution service from a DSP individually. Instead, the Commission ratified an arrangement in
which the 25 owners jointly owned a distribution system operated by one of them as the designated
unitized customer.12 The jointly-owned non-utility distribution system took service at transmission
voltage from Oncor and then distributed electricity to the owners’ wells.13
         In summary, therefore, just as in Flint Hills, a large load customer may legally interconnect
indirectly to the ERCOT system through its self-owned and operated T&D facilities that connect
directly to the facilities of a power generator that is interconnected to the ERCOT system. In areas
with retail customer choice, the purchase of the generator’s output over the customer’s T&D
facilities is legally furnished through a REP and without a DSP. Furthermore, just as in Power
Clearinghouse, if a landlord/tenant relationship exists and any electricity furnished through the
generator’s interconnection to the large load customer is done as an incident of that tenancy without
resale, that is lawful and there is no physical need or legal basis to require the customer to have a
separate relationship or interconnection with a DSP in that arrangement.


   II.          The Commission will serve the public interest by preserving the existing instances
                where a customer may interconnect without a DSP.

         As a matter of policy, the Commission should not undermine its long-established
precedents allowing for fact-specific exceptions to the general framework that relies upon a DSP
to establish retail electric delivery service. First and foremost, the Commission should not
introduce risk to existing self-service and incident of tenancy arrangements that have operated
legally for years.
         Second, the Commission should recognize that customer self-service of this nature
leverages private investment to yield public benefits. A large load customer that takes no DSP
service due to co-location in a net metering arrangement with a generation resource:



         11
              Id., Order at 10 (Finding of Fact 40A).
         12
              Id.
         13
              Id. at 3-4.

Vistra Comments on RAO
Project No. 58481                                                                        Page 6 of 8
         •     must necessarily pay for its own T&D facilities;

        •     must be vetted by the co-located generator (assuring project quality and staking the
              generator’s reputation in the local community on the large load’s responsible
              development);

        •     supports the continued operation of the co-located generator through long-term
              contracting (helping to ensure continued viability, especially of inertia-providing
              thermal dispatchable generation that the ERCOT energy-only market continues to need
              but fails to adequately value);

        •     provides greater operational transparency and visibility to the grid operator through
              the generator’s real-time telemetry; and

        •     through contractual arrangements as well as statutory curtailment provisions in
              PURA §§ 37.0561(e) & 39.169(d), promotes reliability by curtailing the large load and
              in turn making the generation capacity available to the rest of the grid during
              emergencies.
       And, as a matter of practical regulation, if there is no physical or legal requirement to
impose a regulatory restriction, the Commission should avoid doing so because that would
interfere with the pursuit of PURA’s most fundamental policy purpose governing the last quarter
century: that customer choices and the normal forces of competition benefit the public interest
more than the imposition of a regulated monopoly framework.14 And, by contrast, adopting the
policy position in the RAO has no benefit to the ERCOT system or any customer; the only
motivation appears to be to ensure that DSPs can build unnecessary physical facilities that are not
required when a customer invests in its own connecting facilities.
       Finally, it is notable that a large load co-located with a generator is often precluded from
or sharply limited in drawing power via the generator’s interconnection. The FERC order in FERC
Docket No. EL25-49-002 adopted the logical and sensible policy for this scenario—loads that limit
their withdrawals from the grid should not be required to take full grid service—and the
Commission should not take Texas in an opposite direction that puts ERCOT and Texas at a




       14
            PURA § 39.001(a).

Vistra Comments on RAO
Project No. 58481                                                                      Page 7 of 8
 development disadvantage versus the rest of the country while also breaking with PURA, PUCT
rules, and the Commission’s own precedents on such matters.


   III.      The Commission can and should advance new 16 TAC § 25.194 without creating
             a new DSP direct-service requirement.

          Vistra respectfully requests that the Commission revise the RAO rationales and rule text as
necessary to avoid any suggestion or intent that that the large load customer itself must be the
DSP’s retail customer of record or have a direct retail electric service or retail electric delivery
service relationship with the DSP.
          The RAO describes the intermediate agreement as an agreement executed by the large load
customer, the interconnecting DSP, and, if different, the interconnecting TSP, and the SLLIA
similarly assumes DSP participation. The Commission should ensure those provisions are intended
to only require a DSP to be party to the agreement if the large load is taking service from a DSP or
to reflect simply an acknowledgement by the DSP of the process and the arrangement that does
not involve the load taking DSP service.        Ensuring that appropriate intent would harmonize
proposed 16 TAC § 25.194 with existing Texas statutes, Commission rules, and service
arrangements that already recognize the distinction between the entity receiving the utility bill and
the entity ultimately consuming electricity.


Dated: September 8, 2026

                                               Respectfully submitted,

                                               Ned Bonskowski
                                               Vice President, Texas Regulatory Policy

        Power Clearinghouse is especially pertinent in the context of the RAO because it shows
that the distinction between the customer of the utility and the end-use consumer is not an
unintended loophole in current law The Commission considered the actual physical connections
and contractual structure-utility facilities were connected to a master meter, a property owner
purchased utility service, the property owner owned private downstream distribution facilities, and
tenants consumed electricity delivered by the landlord over those facilities-and treated the utility
transaction with the property owner distinctly from the property owner/landlord's relationship with
its tenants/consumers. 16 Tex. Admin. Code ("TAC") § 25.142 provides a similar structure when
a landlord owns submeters. When the landlord owns submeters but the DSP owns the master meter,
electricity reaches and is consumed by the tenant, but the tenant is not the DSP's customer, and the
tenant has no relationship with the DSP. Similarly, in 16 TAC § 25.141 and Tex. Prop.
Code § 92.302, the rule and statute expressly acknowledge that the person with the relationship
with the utility or REP is the "customer" of the utility, while the tenants are the end use consumers
of electricity.
        The provision of electricity as an incident of tenancy is not confined to residential
examples . Request of Trenton View Shopping Center , PUCT Docket No . 36349 , and Application
of San Jacinto Mall Company Against Houston Power Lighting and Power Company,PUCDocket
No. 2822 both involve shopping malls providing power to their tenants as part of the landlord-
tenant relationship. In both of these proceedings, the Commission or Commission Staff determined
that there was no PURA violation associated with the provision of power to the tenants. The fact
patterns in these cases again make clear that the landlord had the direct relationship with the DSP
and the tenants were the ultimate consumers of the power.
        Further highlighting both the lawfulness of customer-owned distribution and the distinction
between the DSP customer and a different end-user, in a case known as "Big Country," the
Commission found no concern with an electricity distribution system being jointly owned by
25 owners serving a unitized oil field operated by one operator who was the DSP's customer. 10
The Commission treated the operator of the unitized oil field as one customer (even though the

          In summary, therefore, just as in Flint Hills, a large load customer may legally interconnect
indirectly to the ERCOT system through its self-owned and operated T&D facilities that connect
directly to the facilities of a power generator that is interconnected to the ERCOT system. In areas
with retail customer choice, the purchase of the generator's output over the customer's T&D
facilities is legally furnished through a REP and without a DSP. Furthermore , just as in Power
Clearinghouse, if a landlord/tenant relationship exists and any electricity furnished through the
generator's interconnection to the large load customer is done as an incident of that tenancy without
resale, that is lawful and there is no physical need or legal basis to require the customer to have a
separate relationship or interconnection with a DSP in that arrangement.


    II.        The Commission will serve the public interest bv preserving the existing instances
               where a customer mav interconnect without a DSP.

          As a matter of policy, the Commission should not undermine its long-established
precedents allowing for fact-specific exceptions to the general framework that relies upon a DSP
to establish retail electric delivery service . First and foremost, the Commission should not
introduce risk to existing self-service and incident Of tenancy arrangements that have operated

legally for years.
          Second, the Commission should recognize that customer self-service of this nature
leverages private investment to yield public benefits. A large load customer that takes no DSP
service due to co-location in a net metering arrangement with a generation resource:

       And, as a matter of practical regulation, if there is no physical or legal requirement to
impose a regulatory restriction, the Commission should avoid doing so because that would
interfere with the pursuit of PURA's most fundamental policy purpose governing the last quarter
century: that customer choices and the normal forces of competition benefit the public interest
more than the imposition of a regulated monopoly framework.14 And, by contrast, adopting the
policy position in the RAO has no benefit to the ERCOT system or any customer; the only
motivation appears to be to ensure that DSPs can build unnecessary physical facilities that are not
required when a customer invests in its own connecting facilities.
       Finally, it is notable that a large load co-located with a generator is often precluded from

their withdrawals from the grid should not be required to take full grid service-and the

   III.      The Commission can and should advance new 16 TAC § 25.194 without creating
             a new DSP direct-service requirement.

          Vistra respectfully requests that the Commission revise the RAO rationales and rule text as
necessary to avoid any suggestion or intent that that the large load customer itself must be the
DSP's retail customer of record or have a direct retail electric service or retail electric delivery
service relationship with the DSP.
          The RAO describes the intermediate agreement as an agreement executed by the large load
customer, the interconnecting DSP, and, if different, the interconnecting TSR and the SLLIA
similarly assumes DSP participation. The Commission should ensure those provisions are intended
to only require a DSP to be party to the agreement if the large load is taking service from a DSP or
to reflect simply an acknowledgement by the DSP of the process and the arrangement that does
not involve the load taking DSP service.        Ensuring that appropriate intent would harmonize
proposed 16 TAC § 25.194 with existing Texas statutes, Commission rules, and service
arrangements that already recognize the distinction between the entity receiving the utility bill and
the entity ultimately consuming electricity.
